Abstract

Managing personal finances has become increasingly complex in modern digital ecosystems where expenditures are fragmented across Unified Payments Interface (UPI) applications, credit cards, debit cards, net banking, and physical cash. Students and young professionals frequently struggle to monitor daily transactions, lacking immediate visibility into remaining monthly allowances and spending velocity.

This project presents SpendWise, a responsive, full-stack financial tracking web application that enables users to record, categorize, audit, and analyze daily spending against an active monthly target budget. SpendWise features a dedicated authentication and user onboarding portal, an interactive real-time dashboard displaying current cycle expenditure, remaining budget thresholds, all-time expenses, and dynamic categorical breakdowns. It provides a searchable, sortable expense ledger with live client filtering, instant CSV spreadsheet export, and a comprehensive reporting engine calculating category share percentages and transaction volume statistics.

A key user-centric innovation implemented in this edition is the zero-budget initial state policy: for newly registered users, the monthly budget is initialized to exactly ₹0.00, prompting users upon first login to explicitly configure their spending ceiling before alerts activate. In rigorous benchmark evaluation using ten standard transactions totaling ₹14,668 against a ₹30,000 allowance, the system precisely calculates budget utilization at 48.9%, leaves a remaining surplus of ₹15,332, and determines an average outlay of ₹1,467 per transaction. The web application is deployed online on Vercel edge infrastructure and includes full offline fallback persistence.

Keywords: Expense Tracker, Personal Finance, Budget Ceiling, Single Page Application (SPA), RESTful Architecture, Spring Boot, React, MySQL, CSV Export.

Chapter 1: Introduction

Course outcomes addressed: CO6 (Problem definition and scope)

1.1 Problem Statement

In contemporary student life and urban workspaces, personal spending occurs rapidly across multiple decentralized channels, including mobile payment wallets (Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm), debit and credit cards, and cash. Without centralized accounting, individuals frequently lose track of small day-to-day expenditures such as food delivery, transit recharges, and utility bills. When funds run low, users face financial stress because they lack visibility into what categories consumed their budget.

Traditional personal accounting applications suffer from steep learning curves, intrusive advertisement clutter, mandatory external bank account linking, or rigid desktop dependencies. SpendWise addresses this challenge by providing a lightweight, high-performance web application that delivers instant expenditure visibility, transparent monthly budget monitoring, categorical aggregation, and offline data privacy without requiring complex server configuration.

1.2 Objectives

The primary objectives of the SpendWise mini project are:

  1. User Onboarding & Session Isolation: Provide secure registration and sign-in capabilities, establishing isolated expense ledgers for distinct accounts.
  2. Active Budget Ceiling Tracking: Allow users to configure a monthly target budget, monitor real-time consumption percentage, and trigger alert banners when thresholds near exhaustion.
  3. Complete Transaction CRUD Operations: Enable users to Create, Read, Update, and Delete expense entries with title, amount, category, date, payment method, and optional remarks.
  4. Multi-Dimensional Search & Filtering: Deliver instant client-side keyword search, categorical filtering, payment channel filtering, chronological sorting, and comma-separated value (CSV) ledger export.
  5. Quantitative Financial Reporting: Compute categorical volume distributions, payment method frequency, spending averages, and generate printable reports.

1.3 Technology Stack

The system is designed with a decoupled multi-tier architecture, permitting portable standalone execution as well as enterprise Spring Boot client-server connectivity:

Layer Technology & Framework Details
Front End (Client SPA) React 18, React Router v7, Modern CSS3 with FinTech Design System (Plus Jakarta Sans, JetBrains Mono, Flexbox, CSS Grid, Glassmorphic headers).
Application Logic JavaScript ES6+ modules with asynchronous data fetching, form validation, filter reducers, and date mathematics.
Backend API (Java) Java 17/21, Spring Boot 3.x, Spring Web MVC (REST Controller), Spring Data JPA, Hibernate ORM (Port 8080).
Database Layer MySQL 8.0 Relational DBMS with InnoDB engine, primary key indexing, and foreign key referential integrity; backed by HTML5 LocalStorage persistence for edge deployment.
Deployment & Tools Vercel Global Edge Network, Git / GitHub, Visual Studio Code, Google Chrome DevTools.

Chapter 2: Requirements

2.1 Users and Functional Requirements

The functional requirements outline the fundamental interactions and services provided by SpendWise to end users:

ID Requirement Description User Role
FR-01 User Registration & Authentication: Create an account with username, full name, email, and password. For all new registrations, the monthly budget must be initialized to ₹0.00. Support password visibility toggling and quick demo logins. User / Admin
FR-02 Record Expense (Create): Log a new spending transaction with title, amount (positive decimal), predefined category, date picker, payment method, and optional notes. User
FR-03 Ledger Audit (Read): View the comprehensive transaction history with formatted Indian Rupee (₹) amounts, category tags, and payment channel badges. User
FR-04 Transaction Modification (Update/Delete): Edit any field of an existing expense or delete the record with confirmation safety dialogs. User
FR-05 Financial Overview Dashboard: Real-time calculation of This Month Spent, Remaining Budget, All-Time Expenses, and dynamic Category Share percentages. User
FR-06 Budget Ceiling Configuration: Edit monthly target budget limit at any time, instantly recalculating remaining surplus and consumption rate. User
FR-07 Multi-Criteria Filtering & Sorting: Instant client-side filtering by description keyword, category dropdown, payment channel, and date/amount sorting. User
FR-08 Data Portability (CSV Export): Generate and download the filtered transaction ledger as a standard CSV spreadsheet file. User
FR-09 Financial Analytics & Printing: Display summary statistics (average transaction size, max expense) and trigger browser print dialog for paper records. User
FR-10 Session Termination (Logout): Invalidate active user session, clear working state, and safely redirect to the sign-in portal. User / Admin

2.2 Non-Functional Requirements

  • Security: All protected views are guarded by client-side routing guards; passwords require a minimum of 6 characters; user data is strictly isolated by user ID.
  • Performance & Responsiveness: Instantaneous reactive DOM updates without full-page refreshes; asynchronous operations complete in under 50ms in browser storage and under 200ms over REST.
  • Usability & Ergonomics: High-contrast modern FinTech color palette (Indigo/Cyan/Emerald); intuitive visual status badges (Green = Safe, Amber = Warning, Red = Exceeded); clean mobile-responsive layout for smartphones, tablets, and desktops.
  • Reliability & Portability: Graceful degradation ensuring that if the local Spring Boot backend is unreachable, client-side persistence seamlessly activates without throwing fatal exceptions.

UNIQUE KEY (email)

UNIQUE KEY (name)
expenses id (BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT), user_id (BIGINT), category_id (INT), title (VARCHAR(150)), amount (DECIMAL(10,2)), expense_date (DATE), payment_method (ENUM), notes (TEXT), created_at (TIMESTAMP) PRIMARY KEY (id)

3.5 Design Choices: Scalability and Maintainability (CO5)

The architecture of SpendWise balances rapid deployment, zero-latency execution, and maintainability:

Design Decision Alternative Considered Justification (Scalability & Maintainability)
Decoupled Single Page Application (SPA) Multi-page server-rendered JSP / Servlet application Eliminates full page reloads, offloads rendering to client browser, reduces server load, and enables seamless deployment to edge CDNs (Vercel).
Dual-Mode Data Layer (REST API + LocalStorage) Strict server-only MySQL dependency Ensures 100% operational reliability. When evaluated offline or on cloud preview, the application operates flawlessly without requiring an active MySQL instance.
Dynamically Computed Aggregates Storing pre-computed running totals in database rows Prevents synchronization anomalies, race conditions, and stale data. Aggregates are computed on-the-fly from granular records using JavaScript array reducers and SQL aggregate functions.
Zero-Budget Initialization Policy Hardcoding arbitrary default budgets (e.g. ₹30,000) Prevents false financial assumptions for new users; forces explicit configuration of target limits, ensuring data integrity.

Chapter 4: Implementation and Testing

Course outcomes addressed: CO3, CO4, CO6

4.1 How the Modules Work

SpendWise is organized into four interconnected functional modules:

  1. Authentication & User Session Module (AuthContext.jsx, LoginPage.jsx): Manages the user lifecycle. Registration validates username uniqueness, email structure, and matching passwords. New users are assigned monthlyBudget = 0.00. Active sessions are stored securely in local storage, allowing instant access across browser reloads.
  2. Dashboard & Metric Computation Module (DashboardPage.jsx): Filters all recorded expenses against the active Gregorian month (YYYY-MM). It computes total monthly outlay, checks against the budget ceiling, evaluates status (Safe, Warning, Exceeded), and formats numbers in Indian numbering format (e.g. ₹14,668). If the budget is ₹0, it displays an interactive configuration banner.
  3. Ledger & Filtering Engine (ExpensesPage.jsx): Applies chained filtering (case-insensitive substring search in titles/notes, category ID matching, payment method selection, and multi-field sorting). It provides a native CSV generator that constructs a Blob and triggers automatic file download.
  4. Transaction Management (CRUD) Module (ExpenseFormPage.jsx): Enforces strict input validation (non-empty title, positive amount, valid date). Handles both creation of new entries and modification of existing records through dynamic route parameters (/edit/:id).

4.4 Runtime Errors Faced and Fixed (CO4)

During the integration of the React frontend, Spring Boot backend, and storage layers, several technical runtime errors were encountered and resolved:

Error / Bug Encountered Root Cause (How Identified) Resolution & Technical Fix
CORS Pre-Flight Rejection
Cross-Origin Request Blocked		 React frontend running on port 5173 was blocked when dispatching asynchronous HTTP requests to Spring Boot on port 8080. Identified via browser console network error. Implemented @CrossOrigin(origins = "*") on Spring REST controllers and configured a global WebMvcConfigurer bean with allowed HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS).
Arithmetic String Concatenation
NaN or "300002450" in Budget		 Form inputs read expense amounts as String types. When performing arithmetic operations (e.g. spent + amount), JavaScript performed string concatenation instead of addition. Enforced explicit numeric type coercion using parseFloat(amount) and Number(val) before executing budget balance and total expenditure calculations.
Infinite JSON Recursion
StackOverflowError		 Bi-directional JPA relationships between the User entity (One-to-Many) and Expense entity (Many-to-One) caused Jackson serializer to loop infinitely during REST serialization. Annotated the User reference in Expense.java with @JsonBackReference and the collection in User.java with @JsonManagedReference to break recursion.
Invalid HTTP 400 on Valid Input
MethodArgumentNotValidException		 Expense date transmitted from HTML <input type="date"> was parsed with timezone offsets, causing validation mismatches against Java LocalDate. Configured ISO-8601 string formatting (YYYY-MM-DD) on the client and annotated the entity field with @JsonFormat(pattern="yyyy-MM-dd").

4.5 Exception Handling Across Layers (CO4)

To prevent unhandled runtime crashes and ensure seamless user feedback, robust exception handling was engineered across all four architectural tiers:

Architectural Layer Exception(s) Intercepted Handling Strategy & User Presentation
Front End (UI/SPA) TypeError, NetworkError, SyntaxError (malformed JSON) Intercepted via try-catch blocks in services; presented to users via floating toast alerts and red banner warnings without freezing the UI.
Controller / Servlet MethodArgumentNotValidException, HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException Captured by centralized @RestControllerAdvice; converts stack traces into structured JSON error payloads returning HTTP 400 Bad Request.
Service Layer ResourceNotFoundException, BudgetExceededException Custom runtime exceptions thrown when an ID does not exist; translated into clear diagnostic messages returned to the caller.
Repository / Database DataIntegrityViolationException, SQLException (duplicate keys) Catches unique constraint violations (e.g. duplicate username); rolls back transactions via @Transactional and returns meaningful HTTP 409 Conflict.

Global Exception Handler Implementation (Spring Boot)

@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> handleValidationExceptions(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
        Map<String, String> errors = new HashMap<>();
        ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().forEach(error -> 
            errors.put(error.getField(), error.getDefaultMessage()));
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST).body(errors);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> handleNotFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) {
        Map<String, String> response = new HashMap<>();
        response.put("error", ex.getMessage());
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND).body(response);
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
    public ResponseEntity<Map<String, String>> handleGeneral(Exception ex) {
        Map<String, String> response = new HashMap<>();
        response.put("error", "An internal error occurred: " + ex.getMessage());
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR).body(response);
    }
}

Chapter 6: Conclusion and References

Course outcomes addressed: CO6

6.1 Conclusion and Future Scope

The SpendWise – Expense Tracker mini project successfully fulfills all objectives stipulated in Chapter 1. The application delivers an intuitive, aesthetically refined, and highly functional solution for personal financial management. Key achievements include:

  • Seamless user authentication with dedicated onboarding where new users are initialized with a strict ₹0.00 budget ceiling.
  • Comprehensive CRUD operations allowing effortless expense creation, real-time auditing, instant editing, and record deletion.
  • Instant multi-criteria search, category filters, payment channel filters, sorting, and CSV data export.
  • Statistical reporting and budget ceiling monitoring, verified accurately with ten benchmark transactions totaling ₹14,668 (48.9% utilization of a ₹30,000 budget, leaving ₹15,332 surplus).
  • Active online cloud deployment accessible to evaluators worldwide at: https://java-miniproject-two.vercel.app.

Future Scope & Enhancements

  1. Automated Bank & SMS Parsing: Integrating Android/SMS reader hooks or Open Banking APIs to automatically log UPI transactions without manual data entry.
  2. Predictive AI Spending Forecasts: Implementing linear regression and time-series analysis to predict end-of-month expenditure based on current spending velocity.
  3. Multi-Currency & Recurring Expenses: Adding support for automated recurring bills (subscriptions) and foreign currency conversions.
  4. Role-Based Family/Group Budgets: Expanding relational schemas to support shared household ledgers with fine-grained access control.
